name: Declension
description: Articles, adjective endings, and case in context.

items.translation: The dog sleeps in the garden.
items.explanation: Nominative subject. The masculine definite article is *der*.

items.translation: The woman sings very beautifully.
items.explanation: Nominative subject. The feminine definite article is *die*.

items.translation: The child plays in the park.
items.explanation: Nominative subject. The neuter definite article is *das*.

items.translation: The children laugh loudly.
items.explanation: Nominative subject. Plural definite article is always *die*, regardless of gender.

items.prompt: Ich sehe {0} Mann auf der Straße.
items.translation: I see the man on the street.
items.explanation: Accusative direct object of *sehen*. Masculine *der* shifts to *den*; feminine, neuter, and plural stay the same.

items.translation: We are visiting the teacher tomorrow.
items.explanation: Accusative direct object of *besuchen*. Feminine *die* stays *die* in the accusative.

items.translation: I am reading the book tonight.
items.explanation: Accusative direct object of *lesen*. Neuter *das* stays *das* in the accusative.

items.translation: He is buying the rolls for us.
items.explanation: Accusative direct object of *kaufen*. Plural *die* stays *die* in the accusative.

items.translation: I am speaking with the teacher.
items.explanation: Dative triggered by *mit*. Masculine *der* → *dem*.

items.translation: I gladly help the young woman.
items.explanation: Dative because *helfen* takes a dative object. Feminine *die* → *der*.

items.prompt: Sie spielt mit {0} Kind im Garten.
items.translation: She plays with the child in the garden.
items.explanation: Dative triggered by *mit*. Neuter *das* → *dem*.

items.prompt: Wir fahren mit {0} Kindern in die Stadt.
items.translation: We are driving with the children into the city.
items.explanation: Dative triggered by *mit*. Dative plural always uses *den*, and the noun gets an *-n* (here *Kindern*).

items.translation: A brother lives in Berlin.
items.explanation: Indefinite nominative; masculine and neuter share *ein*.

items.translation: A cat sits on the chair.
items.explanation: Indefinite nominative feminine takes *eine*.

items.translation: A bicycle stands in front of the house.
items.explanation: Indefinite nominative; masculine and neuter share *ein*.

items.translation: She has a brother in Munich.
items.explanation: Accusative direct object of *haben*. Masculine *ein* → *einen*.

items.translation: I need a new lamp.
items.explanation: Accusative feminine indefinite is *eine* — feminine articles don't change between nominative and accusative.

items.translation: He buys a bread in the morning.
items.explanation: Accusative direct object of *kaufen*. Neuter *ein* stays *ein* in the accusative.

items.translation: We are living with a teacher.
items.explanation: Dative triggered by *bei*. Masculine *ein* → *einem*.

items.translation: I give a sister the present.
items.explanation: Dative indirect object of *geben* (the recipient). Feminine *eine* → *einer*.

items.translation: She helps a child with learning.
items.explanation: Dative because *helfen* takes a dative object. Neuter *ein* → *einem*.

items.translation: No father is at home today.
items.explanation: Negative article *kein* takes the same endings as *ein*. Nominative masculine is *kein*.

items.translation: No lamp is on the table.
items.explanation: Negative article *kein* takes the same endings as *ein*. Nominative feminine is *keine*.

items.translation: No car is in front of the house.
items.explanation: Negative article *kein* takes the same endings as *ein*. Nominative neuter is *kein*.

items.translation: No animals live in this city.
items.explanation: *kein* has plural forms even though *ein* does not. Nominative plural is *keine*.

items.translation: I have no dog at home.
items.explanation: Accusative direct object of *haben*. Masculine *kein* → *keinen* (same endings as *ein*).

items.translation: He drinks no milk for breakfast.
items.explanation: Accusative direct object of *trinken*. Feminine *keine* stays *keine* in the accusative.

items.prompt: Sie liest {0} Buch in den Ferien.
items.translation: She reads no book during the holidays.
items.explanation: Accusative direct object of *lesen*. Neuter *kein* stays *kein* in the accusative.

items.translation: We have no more rolls.
items.explanation: Accusative direct object of *haben*. Plural *keine* stays *keine* in the accusative.

items.translation: She lives with no brother.
items.explanation: Dative triggered by *bei*. Masculine *kein* → *keinem* (same endings as *ein*).

items.translation: I help no lazy sister.
items.explanation: Dative because *helfen* takes a dative object. Feminine *keine* → *keiner*.

items.prompt: Sie spricht mit {0} Kind in der Klasse.
items.translation: She speaks with no child in the class.
items.explanation: Dative triggered by *mit*. Neuter *kein* → *keinem*.

items.prompt: Er spielt mit {0} Tieren im Park.
items.translation: He plays with no animals in the park.
items.explanation: Dative triggered by *mit*. Dative plural is *keinen*, and the noun gets an *-n* (here *Tieren*).

items.translation: A small dog is sleeping here.
items.explanation: Indefinite + adjective: *ein* doesn't show gender here, so the adjective takes the strong masculine nominative ending *-er* (*kleiner*).

items.translation: A young daughter is laughing loudly.
items.explanation: Nominative feminine with *eine*; the adjective takes *-e* (*junge*) since *eine* already marks the gender.

items.translation: A new bicycle is in the yard.
items.explanation: Indefinite + adjective: *ein* doesn't show gender here, so the adjective takes the strong neuter nominative ending *-es* (*neues*).

items.translation: We are looking for an old key.
items.explanation: Accusative masculine direct object of *suchen*: *ein* → *einen*; the adjective then takes *-en* (*alten*).

items.translation: She needs a red flower.
items.explanation: Accusative feminine direct object of *brauchen*: *eine* stays *eine*, and the adjective takes *-e* (*rote*).

items.translation: We are drinking a cold beer.
items.explanation: Accusative neuter direct object of *trinken*: *ein* stays *ein*, so the adjective takes the strong neuter ending *-es* (*kaltes*).

items.translation: We are living with a nice teacher.
items.explanation: Dative triggered by *bei*: masculine *ein* → *einem*; the adjective takes *-en* (*netten*) after a marked article.

items.translation: She plays with a little sister.
items.explanation: Dative triggered by *mit*: feminine *eine* → *einer*; the adjective takes *-en* (*kleinen*) after a marked article.
